title: Miaozhong on Silence
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of letting go and studying the self to forget the self, encouraging listeners to cultivate awareness and openness through Zazen practice. By releasing attachment to thoughts and concepts, we can meet life's challenges with greater clarity and compassion, and find refuge in silence when needed. This approach invites us to explore our relationship with silence as a doorway to knowing the unknowable, rather than relying on words or intellectual understanding.

Can you hear me?
Okay.
Feel free to come closer.
I like an intimate circle.
So I'll be talking tonight, again, about Miaozhong.

For those of you that weren't here for my other talks, she was a 12th century Chinese Buddhist nun and abbess.
I first learned of her many years ago, when *The Hidden Lamp*, a book by Sue Moon and Norman Fischer, first came out, *Stories of Our Women Ancestors*.
There's a story in that book called "Miaozhong's Interview."

If you're wondering why, I encourage you to read the story if you're not familiar with it.
Many of Miaozhong's writings were lost.

This was true of many of our women ancestors, but there were verse commentaries that she wrote on some of the classic Chinese Zen koans that happened to be preserved, and they were compiled by the author of this book, Beata Grant.
When Beata introduced Miaozhong at the beginning of this book, she took some time to translate her first Dharma talk, given after she was installed as an abbess of the Zhaoxiao nunnery in China.
That's what I want to start out by talking about.
I'm not going to read you the translation of the Dharma talk.
It's pretty involved, but a few sentences really popped out at me.
I took inspiration from John Wiley last week, who just took one sentence that popped out at him about the story he was talking about.
I'm going to quote Miaozhong right here.
*Once the essential teaching of [unclear: "Chang"], Chinese Zen, is transmitted, then that of the Buddhist canon, all the Buddhist teachings, is completely finished.
The best of the lot, however, will understand without being told.*
Maybe I'll read that again.
*Once the essential teaching of Zen is transmitted, then that of the Buddhist canon is completely finished.
The best of the lot, however, will understand without being told.*
What I think she's saying is that this teaching is something you can only comprehend through your experience.
You can't get it with words or intellectual studies.
You can memorize the Buddhist canons, but the teachings are just like fingers pointing to the moon, as my teacher often says.
Then Miaozhong continues:
*Even methods powerful enough to shift the place of stars and constellations, even those are no more than the show of empty fists.*
I think she's saying words, methods, techniques for understanding are of little use.
And she continues:
*Sages do not transmit anything, and students toil over forms like monkeys grasping at their reflections.*
Yeah, I can relate to that.
Sages do not transmit anything; you have to find it in yourself.
And students toil over forms.
How many of us find ourselves tripping over our own feet as we toil over these forms?
Am I getting it right?
What happens if I do it wrong and make a mistake in front of everyone?
Or how often are we in the midst of a ritual and then it's like, how do I do this?
Then you find yourself in a new position like a shuso or an ino and you're teaching the forms, and there's a whole other layer of angst and toiling.
What if I don't know the answer to your question?
What if I misinstruct you?
I've done that.
I often tell you.
But sages do not transmit anything.
It's through this toiling that you learn for yourself.
What I hear in Miaozhong's talk, and then reflected in several of her verse commentaries, is the uselessness of words in conveying the Dharma.
Don't rely on this talk.
Don't rely on Miaozhong's talk, or Chris's instruction, or Tim's Dharma class, or any verbal teachings.
The truth is found, I believe she's saying, in the silence.
It can't be uttered.
As soon as we name it, we conceptualize it, and that in itself is a transgression from non-duality to duality.
As soon as we refer to it, whatever it is, right, there's a subject and an object.
We've already separated ourselves from it.
And listen to my language: separate from it.
There's an it and there's a me.
It's over there and I'm over here.
But if we look at the practices that have been handed down to us by our ancestors, they really revolve around silence.
Silent meditation practice, zazen, kinhin, sesshin practice, which is really an immersion in silence.
Have you noticed what happens when you reside among your Dharma brothers and sisters in silence?
Say at a sesshin, there's a particular flavor of connection and intimacy that can only be experienced in the silence.
Maybe you know what I'm talking about.
In my years of sitting with Everyday Zen, I actually lived 50 minutes away.
I would go once a month to our silent one day sitting and once a year to our silent sesshin, and in between, I never saw anybody from the sangha because I didn't live locally.
Because I was raising my children, I was a busy working mom.
The only people I saw socially were other mothers that were bringing their kids to the playground with me.
I didn't have time, as I have time now, to go for a walk with a sangha friend.
Nonetheless, I grew to feel quite intimate, quite loved and in love with the sangha, having only shared silence, one day sittings and sesshins and nothing more social than that.
I remember, when I was writing this talk, this popped into my head.
It was like three or four years after I stopped sitting with Everyday Zen, because there was the pandemic, and then I moved up here.
I went to my teacher's sesshin, a couple of years ago in Arizona.
One of my Dharma brothers from Everyday Zen showed up at the sesshin, and we eyed each other and we both just looked up and hugged each other.
It had been years, and I never talked to him anyway.
I never saw him once socially, but there was so much love in our embrace.
It was a sweet and touching moment.
So there's a lot that can happen without words.
Have you noticed what happens when you emerge from a one day sitting or a sesshin and you begin to talk to people again?
That is an important transition, I think, to pay attention to.
There's a strong pull within to assume your identity once again with the separate self, to resume your usual mode of relating, me to you, I to other.
Something that strikes me about Miaozhong is that she's really a contemporary of Dogen.
She lived at the same time, but not in the same place.
Dogen was primarily in Japan and she was in China.
So I'm quite sure they didn't know each other.
But I keep hearing Miaozhong in Dogen and I keep hearing Dogen in Miaozhong.
Dogen tells us that practice and enlightenment, I personally prefer the word awakening, are the same thing.
Practice is awakening.
In Fukanzazengi, Dogen writes:

*You should therefore cease from practice based on intellectual understanding, pursuing words and following after speech, and learn the backwards step that turns the light inwardly to illuminate yourself.*
Cease from practice based on intellectual understanding, echoing what Miaozhong was saying.
You're not going to get it right up here in your head.
It's in the body.
Buddha at the moment of enlightenment touched the earth, grounded himself.
Ground yourself, settle in the body, as my teacher says, in zazen body.
Cease pursuing words and following after speech, he says.
I think it's an interesting choice of words that he used to make this point.
He uses the words pursuing, right?
Cease pursuing words and following after speech.
Pursuing and following both imply that there's something out there to pursue, to follow, something that we go after out there.
But no, he says, learn the backwards step that turns your light inwardly to illuminate yourself.
Come back to yourself right here, right now.
Just this.
Notice your sensations.
Notice your experience.
My heart is beating a little fast, a little nervous.
Zazen body is the illuminated self.
In the Genjokoan, Dogen tells us to study the self, to forget the self.
Again, study the self like the backwards step.
Everything you seek is right in here.
But he reminds us not to get attached.
Don't hold on to anything.
Study the self to forget the self.
Let it all go.
As soon as you hold on to it, you've created separation.
You're holding on to something.
So I just invite you to take a breath and let go.
Norman Fischer once told me that when we watch the breath, we put our attention, or our emphasis, on the exhale, because it's on the exhale that we're letting go.
What happens?
What do you experience in the exhale, in the letting go?
Maybe a little more space.
Openness, boundlessness, boundarylessness, without boundaries.
The separate self is bounded.
True nature, Buddha nature, is unbounded.
So zazen is like the practice ground for the rest of life.
We exercise those muscles of awareness when we're on our cushion.
We practice there, turning the light inward.
We watch the patterns of our mind, our reactions, our preferences, our likes, our dislikes.
But the real challenge comes in bringing that practice off the cushion and into our home life, our work life, our sangha life, and so forth.
Nonetheless, the practice is the same, maybe a little harder.
Turn the light inward, study the self to forget the self.
So that was kind of a long Dogen tangent.
We're talking about our women ancestors, so I am going to get back to Miaozhong.
*Once the essential teaching of Zen is transmitted, then that of the Buddhist canon is completely finished.
The best of the lot, however, will understand without being told.
Sages do not transmit anything.*
So, back to wordlessness.
I could just end this talk right now.
I didn't even need to start it.
We could sit together in silence.
That's what I think she's telling us.
The Dharma is transmitted in the silence.
This message I see woven into her verse commentaries over and over again, and I just wanted to read you a few because, again, they popped out at me.
It only makes sense to hear the commentary in the context of the koan, so I'll read the koan first.
This one is called "The World Honored One Ascends His Seat."
*One day, the World Honored One, the Buddha, ascended the seat.
When the Great Assembly had gathered and settled, Manjushri struck his [unclear: "gravel"] and said, "Observe deeply the Dharma of the Dharma King.
The Dharma of the Dharma King is like this."
And the [unclear: "word"] World Honored One then came down from his seat.*
*Miaozhong said, "The true teaching has been transmitted in its entirety.
He said nothing."*
And then there's another koan.
*Zhaozhou entered the hall and said, "A gold Buddha does not pass through the furnace.
A wood Buddha does not pass through the fire.
A mud Buddha does not pass through the water.
The real Buddha sits within."*
Miaozhong's response:
*Gold Buddha, wood Buddha, mud Buddha.
Once understood, they can be tossed beyond Jambudvipa.*
Jambudvipa is, in Buddhist cosmology, the continent inhabited by human beings.
So the human realm.
*They can be tossed beyond the human realm.
To go on and talk about the real Buddha within does nothing but show you're already muddle headed.*
That's Miaozhong.
One more, just because I get such a kick out of it, and learn so much.
This is the koan.
*When Linji saw a monk enter the gates, he shouted.*
Miaozhong responds:
*Bellowing and shouting, railing away with the energy of 10,000 men.
Discuss the Buddha Dharma, and you will still miss your move.*
So let's just be quiet together for a minute and listen to the silence.
What do you hear when I stop speaking?
What do you hear in the silence?
There's an old saying, silence speaks louder than words.
You notice there's actually a lot of sounds when we stop and listen to the silence.
What we call silence is actually a relative silence.
In Zen, we practice relative silence by withholding speech.
This is a practice of external silence, when we withdraw from verbal interactions, like in one day sittings and sesshins.
There's a good reason for this practice, as I mentioned.
It really minimizes our engagement with the conditioned self.
It gives us a break from our conditioned or habituated way of relating to others, our habitual patterns in activity and speech.
It gives us a chance to take some space from who I think I need to be in relation to you.
But our practice isn't just an external practice of silence, but also an internal practice of silence.
In zazen, I'm referring to these moments when our mind quiets and we find ourselves sitting in open awareness.
Maybe thoughts arise, and maybe they pass.
Maybe.
But in that moment, you're there, able to meet whatever the moment holds for you.
Shikantaza.
This is what Dogen refers to as dropping body and mind, letting our preconceived notions of self or other drop away.
What happens when your mind grows quiet?
I can hear.
I can see.
I can perceive more clearly.
Sometimes a curiosity emerges.
What now?
I'm not knowing.
Spaciousness, and acceptance.
Compassion.
Love.
Silence is a doorway to know the unknowable, the unspeakable, the mystery of life.
It invites awe, and more subtle levels of awareness.
I listened to a Dharma talk recently by [unclear: "Allard Kieris"] of Shasta Abbey Zen Center.
He says, "Silence helps us listen to the heart, because the heart speaks very quietly.
In the place of silence, we get to know ourselves."
Silence is a door to know the unknowable.
And one more story.
When I was at Green Gulch in 2018 for the January intensive, Reb Anderson was teaching that intensive.
I asked him how I bring my practice to my job at the time, which was managing 44 massage therapists in this big spa.
I had an overwhelming job, and I wasn't really sure how to practice with it.
When I asked, this was his reply: "Take refuge in the silence.
Receive the silence.
Listen to the silence.
Transmit the silence."
When I got home from my January intensive, I made these little cards, and on the cards I wrote down his words.

I placed the cards in key places: on my desk at work, my desk at home, in the bathroom, on my altar, around my space, to remind myself to take refuge in the silence, to receive the silence, to listen to the silence and transmit the silence.
Two years later, when Tim came to California to live with me, the cards were still throughout my space.
He looked at them and he said, "What does this mean to you?"
Which is a really good question.
What does it mean to you?
Our training is often difficult.
When we sit, among other things, we meet our pain, and we're tempted to seek refuge in noise, in distraction.
We live in a culture that actually encourages noise and distraction.
Our various devices, our screens, our obsessions with productivity, accomplishment, substances, our perceived needs.
And more importantly, our preoccupation with getting those needs met.
The grasping.
What is this?
Not that.
It all creates a lot of noise, and it can distract us from our pain.
I don't know about you, but I need reminders.
I need cards placed around my house and my office, strategically.
I need practice.
I need sangha.
We're swimming upstream together.
We support each other.
We support each other in silence.
We support each other in wordlessness.
We support each other in silence.
Thank you for listening.
I'd like to do the after lecture chant after our small group discussions.
I'd like to get into groups of one, two, three.
There'll be a couple groups of two.
I don't want to go into groups of three.
I would rather there weren't a group of four, because we don't have time for four.
A group of three, and there might be two groups of two.
Each person gets five minutes to explore: What is your relationship to silence?
Do you seek out silence?
Do you avoid silence?
And when do you seek refuge in noise?
Do you need to stop the recording?
Yeah.
I can find Zoom on here.
I'll stop the recording.
